answer.label: Not Ernest Hemingway — a 2011 self-help blog line
answer.authorDates: Contemporary self-help writer · co-creator of Marc & Angel Hack Life
answer.sourceLine: There is no Hemingway source for this sentence. Wikiquote files it under “Disputed” ↗, noting that it is claimed to come from Men Without Women but does not appear in that work, and may have originated in a 2011 blogpost by Marc Chernoff. That post, “30 Things to Stop Doing to Yourself” ↗, does carry the sentence word-for-word as item 4 — unquoted, uncredited, and in the author’s own voice.

source.excerpt: 4. Stop putting your own needs on the back burner. — The most painful thing is losing yourself in the process of loving someone too much, and forgetting that you are special too. Yes, help others; but help yourself too.
trail: Wikiquote’s Ernest Hemingway page ↗ lists the sentence under “Disputed”: claimed to be from Men Without Women, but it does not appear in that work; it may have originated in a 2011 blogpost by Marc Chernoff.
Fetching that post ↗ confirms the sentence verbatim as item 4, immediately after the heading “Stop putting your own needs on the back burner.”
On Goodreads, a reader who bought the Men Without Women ebook asked where the passage was ↗; the reply was that it is not in the book, with a pointer to marcandangel.com.
A Hemingway misquote round-up reaches the same conclusion, calling the Men Without Women sourcing “another false quote to the author’s name” ↗ and naming Chernoff’s 2011 post.
source.excerptNote: A fetch of the live post confirms the sentence appears exactly as circulated. It carries no quotation marks, no attribution and no mention of Hemingway — it reads as the blogger’s own copy.

source.rightsNote: This is modern text, not a pre-1931 literary work, so nothing here is public domain. If the line is Marc Chernoff’s — the origin Wikiquote points to, and the earliest appearance we could confirm by fetching — copyright rests with him as the author of the 2011 blog post. Because Wikiquote hedges (“may have originated”), treat the rights holder as probable rather than settled; either way the sentence is 21st-century writing and in copyright.

author.name: Marc Chernoff
author.kicker: Where the words actually came from
author.heading: About the likely author
author.metaLine: Florida-based self-help writer · co-creator of Marc & Angel Hack Life
author.bio: Marc Chernoff writes the personal-development blog Marc & Angel Hack Life with his wife, Angel Chernoff. Penguin Random House ↗ describes the pair as New York Times-bestselling authors of Getting Back to Happy and creators of the blog, “which was recognized by Forbes as ‘one of the most popular personal development blogs.’” Their stock-in-trade is exactly the register this sentence is written in: short, second-person, list-shaped encouragement.

cite.sourceCitation: Traced by Wikiquote to Marc Chernoff, “30 Things to Stop Doing to Yourself,” Marc & Angel Hack Life (blog), December 11, 2011, https://www.marcandangel.com/2011/12/11/30-things-to-stop-doing-to-yourself/. Not found in Ernest Hemingway, Men Without Women (New York: Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1927).

copyAttribution: "The most painful thing is losing yourself in the process of loving someone too much, and forgetting that you are special too." — not Ernest Hemingway. Wikiquote lists it as disputed: it is claimed to come from Men Without Women (1927) but does not appear in that work, and may have originated in Marc Chernoff's blog post "30 Things to Stop Doing to Yourself" (Marc & Angel Hack Life, 11 December 2011), where it appears verbatim as item 4. Verified at quotle.info.

misattribution.heading: How it got pinned on Hemingway
misattribution.intro: The line circulates almost everywhere with a book attached, which is what makes it convincing — and the book is the part that falls apart first.

items.why: Wikiquote’s Ernest Hemingway page ↗ places the sentence in its “Disputed” section and records that it may have originated in a 2011 blogpost by Marc Chernoff. No Hemingway novel, story, letter or interview containing the wording has been produced.

Quote sites routinely stamp the line with this title — Goodreads credits it to Hemingway, Men Without Women ↗. Wikiquote states plainly that it does not appear in that work, and a reader who searched the ebook could not find it either ↗.

“You are special too” belongs to modern self-help, not to the prose of Men Without Women, whose fourteen stories are bullfight, boxing and war pieces published by Charles Scribner’s Sons in October 1927 ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The best-supported account is the simplest one: it is the fourth item on a self-help list, where it reads “Stop putting your own needs on the back burner” ↗ — and the sentence follows as the writer’s own.

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Hemingway
lead: Hemingway (1899–1961) is one of the internet’s most reliable magnets for sentences he never wrote — the Hemingway Society keeps a page ↗ about the problem, and found that of a batch of twenty-two circulating “Hemingway” quotations, only about half could actually be attributed to him. His name confers gravity on anything short and wounded-sounding.

This line, though, is not built like Hemingway. It is a compound sentence of abstractions — the most painful thing, losing yourself, you are special too — where his published prose leans on concrete nouns and flat declaratives. The tell is the last clause: “you are special too” is the vocabulary of twenty-first-century self-esteem writing, and that is precisely where a fetch of the source lands it.
context.detailsSummary: What Men Without Women actually contains
detailsBody: Men Without Women was published in October 1927 by Charles Scribner’s Sons and collects fourteen stories — among them “The Undefeated,” “In Another Country,” “Hills Like White Elephants,” “The Killers” and “Now I Lay Me” ↗. It is a book of bullfighters, boxers, soldiers and terse dialogue, with no first-person advice to the reader anywhere in it.

A reader who went looking did the obvious thing: bought the ebook and searched it ↗, asking on Goodreads for the passage and chapter. The answer came back that the line is not in the book, with a pointer to marcandangel.com.
context.pull: “Stop putting your own needs on the back burner” is a blog subhead, not a line from a 1927 short-story collection.
